subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Gain Frames vs. Loss Frames
description: A 60-second lesson on Gain Frames vs. Loss Frames.

hook.text: 'This surgery has a 90% survival rate' and 'this surgery has a 10% mortality rate' feel worlds apart. Same data.

buildup.text: Gain frames emphasize what you keep. Loss frames emphasize what you lose. Each activates different emotions.

discovery.text: Gain frames promote caution and acceptance. Loss frames promote fear and action.

twist.text: Health campaigns use loss frames: 'not screening could cost your life.' Fear motivates action better than hope.

climax.text: Every piece of information is framed. The question is: does the frame serve truth or the speaker's agenda?

punchline.text: Frame shapes feeling. Feeling shapes choice.

quiz.question: When do loss frames work best?
options: When you want people to stay calm
When you want to motivate action through fear

details.summary: The same information can be framed as a gain or a loss, producing dramatically different decisions. People tend to be risk-averse when options are framed as gains and risk-seeking when the same options are framed as losses.
details.whyItMatters: Framing is one of the most powerful tools in communication, marketing, and policy. The same surgery described as having a 90 percent survival rate feels safer than one with a 10 percent mortality rate, despite identical information.
takeaways: Gain frames make people risk-averse, preferring certain outcomes
Loss frames make people risk-seeking, preferring gambles
Identical information produces opposite decisions depending on framing

faq.question: How do advertisers use gain and loss framing?
faq.answer: Health products use loss frames like 'don't miss out on protection' because fear motivates action. Luxury products use gain frames like 'treat yourself to something special' because positive emotion drives aspiration purchases.

faq.question: Can awareness of framing effects reduce their impact?
faq.answer: Somewhat. Reframing both ways before deciding helps. But framing effects are remarkably persistent even when people know about them, because the emotional response to a frame happens before conscious correction can occur.
